/about/.description: About Arrownex, the AI for Public Purpose Lab and the named leadership behind MIZAN.
/about/.visibleText: About Connecting AI delivery with institutional responsibility MIZAN is being developed through Arrownex's AI for Public Purpose Lab in the UAE. The Lab brings applied research and institutional assurance into practical AI delivery for government and regulated organisations. People Named leadership behind MIZAN TM Tariq Makadi Co-founder and institutional governance lead. Brings experience in privacy, AI governance and digital public infrastructure to MIZAN's design. As a doctoral researcher at UCL's Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose, he researches the relationship between digital infrastructure, institutions and legitimacy. SK Sujit Kumar Co-founder and Arrownex delivery lead. Leads Arrownex's technology delivery, partnerships and customer relationships, connecting the venture to engineering and operational capability. Operating relationships Arrownex, the Lab and institutional responsibility Arrownex provides the operating and delivery platform. The AI for Public Purpose Lab develops and tests the methods and product proposition. The institution using MIZAN keeps responsibility for its AI approval decisions. Any IIPI relationship statement should be confirmed before stronger public wording is used. No endorsement, backing or institutional partnership is implied here.

/how-it-works/.title: How It Works | MIZAN
/how-it-works/.description: The six-step MIZAN workflow for evidence-backed AI approval decisions.
/how-it-works/.visibleText: How it works From evidence to accountable authorisation The same six steps appear across the site: Define, Evidence, Assess, Authorise, Monitor and Reauthorise. The example below follows a student support assistant (constructed). Six-step workflow The human decision point stays visible Step 1 Define What you bring: Purpose, owner, permitted actions and limits. Who is involved: Service owner and governance lead. What MIZAN produces: A bounded use case and draft approval scope. Step 2 Evidence What you bring: Policies, privacy review, security review, accessibility testing and source list. Who is involved: Evidence owners and specialist teams. What MIZAN produces: A connected evidence set with source and review status. Step 3 Assess What you bring: The connected evidence set and identified gaps. Who is involved: Relevant specialists and accountable reviewers. What MIZAN produces: Findings, unresolved gaps and required conditions. Step 4 Authorise What you bring: Specialist findings and proposed conditions. Who is involved: An authorised institutional decision owner. What MIZAN produces: A worded decision, reasons, conditions and review date. Step 5 Monitor What you bring: Agreed signals such as source changes, incidents and complaints. Who is involved: Operational owner with escalation routes. What MIZAN produces: Signals attached to the relevant part of the approval. Step 6 Reauthorise What you bring: Affected evidence and change history. Who is involved: Decision owner with relevant reviewers. What MIZAN produces: Continue, restrict, suspend or withdraw the approval. Running example Student support assistant (constructed) The assistant answers routine student questions using approved institutional information. Staff handle ambiguous questions and consequential decisions. The approval record defines the assistant's boundaries, evidence and review triggers. Discuss a pilot Illustrative concept using sample information. It does not represent a live deployment. Student support assistant (constructed) AI use Student support assistant for routine questions. Purpose Answer questions using approved institutional information. Accountable owner Student services lead. Allowed Use approved sources and draft support responses. Not allowed Decide eligibility, discipline, progression or access to services. Evidence Source accuracy, student data protections, accessibility, staff readiness. Decision Authorised, with conditions Conditions Escalate ambiguous questions and consequential decisions to staff. Review date 30 January 2027. Material change When the use changes, the permission comes back for review If the assistant is proposed to start making eligibility decisions, the original guidance-only approval must be reassessed. The affected evidence, human decision boundary and accountable owner return to review before any new approval is recorded. Possible outcomes Continue, restrict, suspend or withdraw the approval. The outcome is recorded in words with the reason and review date, not as a score.

/.title: MIZAN | Clear, Accountable Decisions About AI Use
/.description: MIZAN brings together evidence, expert review and human approval for specific institutional AI uses.
/.visibleText: AI assurance for public institutions Clear, accountable decisions about AI use MIZAN brings together evidence, expert review and human approval for a specific AI use. It records who approved it, what the AI may do, the conditions attached, and when the decision needs review. AI assurance means checking and documenting whether an AI use is fit for its purpose and its operating conditions. Discuss a pilot See an example In development. Exploring a focused design-partner pilot. Illustrative concept using sample information. It does not represent a live deployment or final product interface. Example approval record AI use Resident service assistant (constructed) Purpose Explain published requirements and route complex cases to staff. Accountable owner Service delivery director Decision Authorised, with conditions Review date 30 January 2027 Example record What an accountable AI approval can look like The decision state is word-based, not a score. The example separates what the AI may do, what remains a human decision, which evidence was reviewed, and when the approval needs review. Illustrative concept using sample information. It does not represent a live deployment or final product interface. Resident service assistant (constructed) AI use Resident-facing assistant for a public service. Purpose Explain published requirements, help residents prepare information, and route complex cases. Accountable owner Service delivery director. Allowed Use approved guidance, draft explanations, route cases to staff. Not allowed Make eligibility decisions, change records, or send final notices. Evidence Service policy, privacy and security review, accessibility testing, answer-quality review. Decision Authorised, with conditions Conditions Staff review for ambiguous cases; complaint signals trigger review. Review date 30 January 2027. Benefits Why institutions use an approval record P Make responsibility clear. Name the person responsible for the approval and the people who review the evidence. D Keep the basis for approval together. Link the decision to the assessments, policies and conditions that support it. C Know when to review. Flag changes that may affect the approval and route them for human review. The problem AI approval depends on more than a technical test An AI system may perform well while important questions remain unanswered: who can approve its use, can the organisation supervise it, what must stay a human decision, and what happens if the system or its purpose changes. Evidence spread across teams. Policies, tests and reviews often sit in different documents and systems. Unclear basis for approval. A decision may be recorded without a clear link to its evidence, limits and owner. Changes after launch. A new model, policy, permission or incident may require the original decision to be reviewed. How it works From evidence to a decision people can stand behind MIZAN is designed to reuse your existing governance work and connect it to a maintained decision record. The institution keeps responsibility for the approval. 01 Define Set the purpose, responsible owner, permitted actions and limits. 02 Evidence Bring together existing policies, assessments, technical tests and operational information. 03 Assess Ask relevant specialists to review the evidence and identify gaps or conditions. 04 Authorise An authorised person records the reasons, conditions and review date. 05 Monitor Track agreed changes and signals that could affect the basis for approval. 06 Reauthorise Decide whether to continue, restrict, suspend or withdraw the approval. See the full workflow Where MIZAN sits Not another AI governance dashboard AI governance platforms check whether an AI system is tested, monitored and under policy control. MIZAN answers a narrower, later question: given that evidence, is this institution currently entitled and able to let this specific AI act on its behalf, and for how long. MIZAN sits after AI governance, not instead of it. AI governance and assurance tools Is the system safe, tested and monitored? → MIZAN Is the institution entitled to let it act, right now? See how MIZAN relates to existing tools People and public purpose Keep people in control of consequential decisions Public service AI should stay understandable, accessible and open to challenge. The approval record should define when staff must intervene, what decisions remain with people, and how concerns reach the responsible team. Material change A material change is a change that could affect the basis for approval, such as a model update, a permission change, or a rise in complaints. Use cases Start with one clearly defined AI use Government services. Define how a service assistant may explain guidance, support staff and route complex cases, while keeping final decisions with authorised officers. Allowed Explain published guidance. Not allowed Make eligibility decisions. Education. Set clear boundaries for a student support assistant, including approved sources, escalation to staff and decisions it cannot make. Allowed Answer routine questions. Not allowed Make consequential decisions. Explore use cases Credibility and development Applied research connected to practical delivery MIZAN is being developed through Arrownex's AI for Public Purpose Lab in the UAE. The work combines institutional governance, privacy and public policy expertise with engineering and security delivery. The methodology draws on public sector guidance and research on accountability, institutional capability and AI assurance. Pilot work will test whether the approach produces clearer decisions, reuses existing evidence and identifies when review is needed. Arrownex Delivery. AI for Public Purpose Lab Method. UCL IIPP Doctoral research, individual affiliation. Build the first case around your institution Start with one AI use, one accountable owner and an agreed operating environment. Together, we can map the evidence, define the conditions for approval and agree how the pilot's value will be measured. What we would agree: scope and responsibilities; evidence and review requirements; pilot deliverables and acceptance criteria. Discuss a pilot FAQ Quick answers before you read further What does MIZAN do? MIZAN records the evidence, conditions, owner, approval decision and review date for a specific institutional AI use. Who makes the approval decision? The institution does. MIZAN is designed to make the decision basis clear and reviewable; it does not grant legal or statutory authority. Does it replace our existing assessments? No. MIZAN is designed to reuse evidence from existing risk, privacy, security and AI evaluation work. Is this only for AI agents? No. The method is useful wherever an institution needs a clear approval basis, bounded permissions, human supervision and review. Can we use it today? MIZAN is in development and exploring focused design-partner pilots. A pilot would start with one clearly defined AI use. How would a pilot begin? We would agree the scope, responsible owner, evidence to review, conditions to test, and how value will be measured.

/platform/.title: Platform | MIZAN
/platform/.description: One record for evidence, approval and review of institutional AI use.
/platform/.visibleText: Platform One record for evidence, approval and review MIZAN is being developed to help institutions connect an AI use to the evidence, people and conditions that support its approval. The record is designed to stay reviewable as the system and its operating environment change. Discuss your requirements See the example workflow Illustrative concept using sample information. It does not represent a live deployment. Resident service assistant (constructed) AI use Resident-facing service assistant. Purpose Explain published requirements and route complex cases to staff. Accountable owner Service delivery director. Allowed Explain guidance, prepare drafts, route cases. Not allowed Make eligibility decisions or change official records. Evidence Service policy, privacy and security review, accessibility testing, answer quality. Decision Authorised, with conditions Conditions Staff review ambiguous cases; complaints trigger review. Review date 30 January 2027. Core capabilities What the platform helps you check and record Define the approval. Record the purpose, responsible owner, permitted actions, limits and review date. Connect the evidence. Link policies, assessments and technical reports to the question each item supports. Record specialist review. Keep specialist findings, unresolved gaps and required conditions visible to the decision owner. Check organisational capability. Assess mandate, people, processes, data controls, supervision, transparency, contestability and monitoring for this use. Review changes. Connect agreed change signals to the parts of the approval that need reassessment. Recover the history. Show what was known, what was reviewed, who decided, and the conditions attached. Working with existing systems Designed to use the evidence institutions already hold MIZAN is designed to use evidence from existing risk, privacy, security and AI evaluation processes. Integration and deployment requirements should be agreed for each pilot, including identity, permissions, hosting, data access and change monitoring. Available now Structured approval record Manual evidence mapping and review fields for focused pilot use. In development Evidence import workflow Connector requirements to be agreed during pilot scoping. Planned Change monitoring signals Signal design depends on deployed systems and permissions. Planned Identity and permissions Deployment-specific integration, not presented as live today. AI governance relationship A different question from the AI governance layer AI governance platforms such as Credo AI and IBM watsonx.governance are built to answer whether an AI system is tested, monitored and compliant, and both describe themselves that way. MIZAN does not compete with that layer. It starts from its output and asks whether the institution is currently entitled to rely on it for one specific use. Platform What they say about themselves What they track The question they answer Credo AI "AI Governance, Built for the Agentic Era" and "Measurable Trust for Every AI System" The AI system, agent, model and vendor Is this AI trustworthy and under policy control? IBM watsonx.governance "Govern smarter. Scale faster." and "Continuous accountability" The AI use case, across its lifecycle Is this AI documented, monitored and compliant? MIZAN "Clear, accountable decisions about AI use" The institution's permission to use it, for this specific case Is this institution entitled, right now, to let this AI act? Quoted from each platform's own public homepage or product page, fetched 30 September 2026. Shown for factual comparison only, not as a ranking. MIZAN is designed to complement AI governance and assurance tools, not replace them. How the record is assembled Evidence and approval flow into one maintained record 01 Policy Applicable rules, public purpose and operating constraints. 02 Capability Institutional readiness, people, supervision and escalation. 03 System assurance Tests, privacy, security and operational evidence. 04 Authorisation Named decision, conditions and review date. See the full workflow

/research/.title: Research and Method | MIZAN
/research/.description: Research and method for evidence-backed institutional AI approval decisions.
/research/.visibleText: Research and method A practical method for evidence-backed AI decisions Our research asks how institutions can connect AI evidence to a clear human decision, sustain supervision, and recognise when an approval needs review. The method is being developed and tested against specific institutional use cases. Initial notes Three method notes for early readers What an AI approval record should contain Author: MIZAN research team. Date: 1 October 2026. Distinguishes proposed record fields from findings still being tested. When an approval needs review Author: MIZAN research team. Date: 1 October 2026. Sets out change triggers such as new permissions, model changes and complaints. How to test institutional capability for one AI use Author: MIZAN research team. Date: 1 October 2026. Frames capability as use-specific evidence, not a maturity score. What the evidence says Public guidance converges on named accountability, bounded permissions and review Public bodies researching AI governance, among them the World Bank, the OECD, the UK government and Canada's federal AI guidance, converge on the same requirements: named accountability, bounded permissions, ongoing monitoring, and the ability to pause or withdraw an AI use. MIZAN's method is designed around that convergence. Cited for context only; no endorsement, certification or formal partnership is implied. Assurance Watch Assurance Watch A manually maintained, reverse-chronological editorial log of developments in institutional and agentic AI assurance. This is not a live feed and no endorsement is implied. 25 Sep 2026 OECD, Governing with Agentic AI in Government Argues that governance cannot rely only on broad principles or after-the-fact review alone, and documents real public-sector approaches to authorising agentic AI. What it means for MIZAN: Supports continuous, built-in authorisation rather than a one-off sign-off. Primary source Cited for context only; no endorsement, certification or formal partnership is implied. 15 Sep 2026 Canada, Guide on the Use of Agentic Artificial Intelligence Requires bounded autonomy, designated accountable owners, logging and recoverability, and names automation drift as a risk to monitor. What it means for MIZAN: Close correspondence to MIZAN's boundary and named-holder design. Primary source Cited for context only; no endorsement, certification or formal partnership is implied. 1 Apr 2026 UK, Digital Assurance Playbook and Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Moves departmental digital and AI assurance toward owned, published records. What it means for MIZAN: MIZAN is designed to reuse ATRS-style records as evidence, not duplicate them. Digital Assurance Playbook · ATRS guidance Cited for context only; no endorsement, certification or formal partnership is implied. 2026 BCS-led AI assurance consortium A UK government-convened programme on professional competence, ethics and information access for AI assurance. What it means for MIZAN: Relevant to Mu'tamad's question of reviewer and supervisor competence. Primary source Cited for context only; no endorsement, certification or formal partnership is implied. 1 Sep 2026 NPL, Call for Evidence on AI testing, evaluation and assurance A measurement-focused programme for AI testing, evaluation and assurance in the UK. What it means for MIZAN: Relevant to evidence quality, not to institutional authorisation directly. Primary source Cited for context only; no endorsement, certification or formal partnership is implied. Research attribution Research context is not product endorsement The founder's UCL research can inform the product thesis. Public guidance from the World Bank, OECD, UK and Canada can inform requirements. Neither constitutes product endorsement. BCS and NPL pathways need precise, dated descriptions of their actual status before use.
